title: A month without food
about: What happens to the worms when nobody feeds them, and how would you notice? A helper feeds the box for a week so the feeder learns how much the worms eat. Then a month without food: cocoons stop, the worms thin out slowly (they live on the bedding a while), and with leave to go some go into the bed. When feeding starts again, they eat much less than before, with food lying there: the keeper's "dying back" notice. No sensor counts worms; the feeder reads it from the weight.

steps.title: A week of feeding, at an hour a second
steps.why: The helper feeds each morning what was eaten. The feeder watches the box get lighter and reckons how many worms are working: worms eat about half their weight a day. It needs several weighings a day, so the clock runs at one hour a second here (a week takes under three minutes).

expect.say: the feeder reckons {v} kg of worms

steps.title: You go away for a month
steps.why: No food and no one to water: the clock runs at five hours a second. Laying stops within days. The worms get hungry slowly (they eat the bedding a while), but the bin also dries out, and dryness drives them out or kills them faster than hunger.

steps.title: Back home: feeding again
steps.why: Food again, at an hour a second so the feeder can weigh. They eat much less than before the month away although food lies there. The keeper compares the feeder's estimate with a week and more ago and tells you that fewer worms are working.

steps.title: Back to normal
steps.why: The helper stops and the clock runs at its usual pace. Given food, the worms recover over the next weeks.
